what_it_does: Many scientific and engineering simulations (fluid flow, structural analysis, machine learning) need to solve large systems of linear equations, and a family of algorithms called Krylov subspace methods (iterative solvers that progressively home in on a solution) are the standard tool. These methods repeatedly multiply a sparse matrix (a grid of numbers where most entries are zero) by a vector — an operation called SpMV (sparse matrix-vector multiply). A useful speedup called a matrix-power kernel batches several of these multiplications together so that the matrix's data can be reused from the processor's fast local memory (cache) rather than re-fetched from the large, slow main memory chip (DRAM) each time. The problem is that data dependencies between rows of the matrix block this reuse, and symmetric matrices create additional conflicts when multiple processor cores try to update shared results simultaneously. This paper, Me-MPK, builds a dependency graph that captures all these conflicts, then recursively splits the problem into independent sub-problems that can run in parallel without conflicts, maximizing cache reuse while eliminating the need for expensive synchronization between cores.
